newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Assembly won't take up securitization bil.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Assembly won't take up securitization bil.

text.p: The New York Assembly will not take up Gov. George Pataki's proposal to securitize stranded costs of the state's electric utilities, Speaker Sheldon Silver told Reuters.
Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc has said securitization, as proposed by Pataki and passed by the state Senate, has the potential to reduce its rates 5 percent.
Other utilities that would be affected by the change include Long Island Lighting Co, Orange & Rockland Utilities Inc, Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp and Niagara Mohawk Power Corp.
The other two are New York State Electric & Gas Corp and Rochester Gas & Electric Corp.
The Assembly "will not take up the bill as presently composed," Silver said, explaining it "benefits only stock holders" of the utilities.
The speaker said he would support limited securitization as part of comprehensive legislation designed to provide a base for restructuring of the utility industry and the state's regulatory efforts.
In particular, he cited the Competition Plus/Energy 2000 proposal that passed the Assembly in June 1996.
Earlier, he told visting legislators the goal of this proposal was move New York's electric rates closer toward the national average by reducing them 25 percent statewide.

The New York Assembly was one sponsorer of the conference -- entitled "The Electric Industry in the Balance: The Legislative Role for Reform." The meeting was also sponsored by the National Conference of State Legislatures with the National Council on Competition and the Electric Industry.

"Reducing electricity rates is everybody's goal, and virtually everyone agrees that establishing a compeititive market for electricity is the way to do it," Silver pointed out in his welcoming remarks.
"Yet, this seemingly straightforward goal presents complex problems."

In New York, he said, efforts of the Public Service Commission to move the state into a competitive power market "have produced enormous public controversies over the size and distribution of rate cuts, consumer protection issues and whether the PSC is creating a level playing field within the electricity industry.
"If nothing else, these controversies demonstrate the need for a comprehensive, well-thought out policy," he concluded.
